title: Starry spin-up
caption: Star trails over La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Circles of starlight wheel around the south celestial pole, seen directly overhead at ESO's La Silla Observatory in this dizzying photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Alexandre Santerne. At first glance it could pass for an optical illusion or an abstract painting.

Each circular streak is one star, recorded over a long period so that its apparent motion across the sky, caused by the Earth's rotation, becomes visible. La Silla sits on the outskirts of Chile's Atacama Desert some 2400 metres up, and enjoys over 300 clear nights a year, ideal for long exposures like this.

Several telescopes appear near the bottom. The ESO 3.6-metre telescope stands on the left peak and hosts HARPS, the High Accuracy Radial velocity Planet Searcher, which ESO calls the world's foremost extrasolar planet hunter. The New Technology Telescope partly hides it, and the silver-domed MPG/ESO 2.2-metre is visible too.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure landscape photograph at ESO's La Silla Observatory, in visible light. The exact camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points; only a long exposure turns the Earth's rotation into these circular trails.

explore: Other telescopes in view include the Swiss 1.2-metre Leonhard Euler Telescope, the ESO 1-metre Schmidt, the Danish 1.54-metre and the ESO 1.52-metre.
ESO ranks La Silla just behind the VLT among the world's most scientifically productive ground-based observatories, with almost 300 refereed publications a year.
alt: Concentric circular star trails filling the sky above several telescope domes on a mountain.
